chunks: What inductor cores do. The question: What do cores do on inductors?
A core is a chunk of magnetic material, like ferrite, that the coil's wire is wrapped around. It guides the magnetic field and concentrates it.
That lets the same number of turns give far more inductance, so inductors can be smaller. The price is that cores can fill up (saturate) and waste some energy as heat.
Think of a river and a concrete channel. Spilled water spreads out in all directions. Put it in a channel and all of it follows one path.
A core is the channel for the magnetic field: air lets the field spread out weakly, while the core guides it along a strong path. A channel can only carry so much, though.

In an air-core coil (left, orange turns) the flux returns through the surrounding space (long, wide path, high reluctance), while a closed high-permeability core confines nearly all of it to a short, well-defined path (dashed line inside the blue ring).
The orange bars across the toroid are the winding turns.
Magnetic flux: the amount of magnetic field the coil and core carry. Permeability ( micro ): how well a material carries magnetic flux. Higher means a stronger guide.
Reluctance: how much a flux path resists carrying flux. Inductance equals the number of turns squared ( N squared ) divided by the reluctance.
Saturation: the core cannot carry any more flux. Air gap: a deliberate cut in the core that lowers inductance but lets it carry more current.
Wind the same coil twice. In air, you get some inductance, call it L 0 . Now put it on a ferrite core with a relative permeability of 2000.
The inductance rises by about a factor of 2000, so L is roughly 2000 times L 0 . You can get a target inductance with far fewer turns. That is the whole idea.
"A core is magnetic material, ferrite or powdered iron, that concentrates the flux.

Inductance goes as turns squared over reluctance, and a high-permeability core has far lower reluctance than air, so you get hundreds or thousands of times more inductance from the same turns, in less space.
The costs are saturation, where inductance collapses at high current, and core loss. An air gap lowers the inductance but raises the saturation current and stores the energy."
